The app is designed to be "locally aware" to show you relevant news and maps immediately. Timezone-Based Region: It uses the Intl.DateTimeFormat() API to see your timezone. This allows it to center the map on your part of the world (e.g., Europe vs. Asia) without ever asking for your GPS coordinates. Browser Language: It checks your browser's language settings (e.g., Greek, Korean, or Arabic) to automatically enable native-language news feeds and AI-translated summaries. Precise GPS (Opt-in): Only if you explicitly grant permission, the browser's Geolocation API can be used to center the map on your exact coordinates. As of early 2026, the developer (Elie Habib) and the system's AI algorithms have prioritized the Iran-Israel conflict because it is currently the most "active" theater for the types of data the app tracks. Here is the breakdown of why it stays pinned to the top: The app uses a Convergence Model. It looks for multiple different signals happening in the same place at the same time. Currently, Iran has a high concentration of: Military Flight Activity: Live ADS-B data showing an unusual number of tanker or transport planes. Satellite Thermal Alerts: NASA FIRMS data detecting "heat signatures" (fires or explosions) that the AI correlates with recent news. GPS Jamming: High levels of interference in the region that the app maps in real-time. News Velocity: A massive volume of RSS feeds and official statements currently mention Iran more frequently than other regions. Hidden aircraft When an aircraft turns off its GPS broadcast or uses a "non-cooperative" transponder, the app uses three main methods to track it The app pulls data from a network of ground receivers. When four or more receivers pick up the same "blind" signal, the system calculates the Time Difference of Arrival (TDOA). If a "ghost" plane disappears or its GPS signal starts jumping wildly (spoofing), the app looks at the Navigation Integrity Category (NIC) value sent by other nearby planes. It then overlays a "red zone" on the map. If you see a cluster of flights suddenly behaving strangely or disappearing in a red zone, it's a strong indicator of electronic warfare or "dark" military flights in that corridor. The app's creator, Elie Habib, designed it to look for "overlapping signals." If a plane goes dark (transponder off), the app doesn't just give up. It looks for other clues: Satellite Thermal Alerts: It checks NASA's FIRMS data for heat signatures (jet engine exhaust or flares) in areas where planes just "vanished." Ground-Based OSINT: It scans Telegram and social media feeds for "citizen intelligence"people reporting the sound of low-flying jets or sightings that match the last known trajectory of a dark flight. Infrastructure Anomalies: It monitors if specific military airbases suddenly show high activity or if civilian airports report mass cancellations, which often precedes "dark" military movements. Direct Radar Feeds (ADSB-Exchange) Unlike commercial apps (like FlightRadar24) that often censor or hide military aircraft at the request of governments, World Monitor often pulls from unfiltered sources like ADSB-Exchange. This means it shows many aircraftincluding "blocked" private jets and some military transportsthat other apps intentionally scrub from their displays. Note https://www.worldmonitor.app/ Web Version: Uses cloud-based AI (like Groq or OpenRouter) to summarize news. Your browser sends the headlines to their servers to get the "World Brief." Windows Version: It can connect to a local AI runner like Ollama or LM Studio on your PC. This means the AI analysis happens entirely on your own hardware. Big thanks to https://github.com/wh1te4ever/super-tart-vphone-writeup and https://github.com/Lakr233/vphone-cli. This is a real virtual machine running iOS 26.1, no streaming, no emulation, etc. Should be jailbreakable, but I'm lazy. This is possible because Apple included firmware of the "iPhone Virtual Research Environment" device with the recent cloudOS release, with some hacks and firmware mixing (cloudOS is based on iOS) it actually boots up to the GUI albeit with broken GPU acceleration due to missing ParavirtGPU MTL compiler plugin - fixable!!! iPhone VRE itself is based on vresearch1 machine which is included with macOS since 15.1. Uses Virtualization.framework, so obviously not compatible with other OSes and Intel Macs. Use Inferno (QEMUAppleSilicon), it boots iOS14 (and 15 apparently too) now.
